newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian soldiers recount shooting of Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian soldiers recount shooting of Israelis.

text.p: Army comrades of a Jordanian soldier charged with premeditated murder of seven Israeli schoolgirls told a military court on Monday they saw him shooting volleys of automatic fire at the young girls.
The three soldiers, the first witnesses in the trial of Private Ahmed al-Daqamsa, told a five-man army tribunal that Daqamsa threatened to shoot them too when they tried to intervene.

"I heard shooting... I saw Ahmed Daqamsa pointing his rifle at the Israeli girls and shooting at them," Private Bilal Hassan told the court while Daqamsa looked on from behind the black bars of a cage inside the court.
"He said: I'll shoot anyone who gets near me... You're all cowards," Hassan said. He said Daqamsa carried on firing until his rifle jammed.

Three of Daqamsa's relatives were thrown out of court for shouting their support during the heated court session and Daqamsa, wearing an olive-green army jumpsuit, was warned by tribunal head Brigadier Mamoun al-Khasawneh for his outbursts.
Daqamsa, who could face the death penalty for his March 13 attack, was applauded by his relatives after the hearing.
"God is with you Ahmed," shouted his wife.
Defence lawyer Hussein al-Majalli tried to throw doubt on the prosecution case that Daqamsa -- known in his army unit as "Ahmed Sex" -- was an amoral assassin who had planned the shooting for months.
Daqamsa's lawyers have portrayed him as a pious man who prayed regularly and opened fire on the schoolgirls, aged 11 to 13, in a fit of anger after they started teasing him.

Daqamsa shot the girls in the Jordanian border area of Baqoura leased to Israel under a 1994 peace accord and has since become a celebrity for opponents of the accord, who view the lease deal as a surrender of Jordanian territory.
Majalli, head of Jordan's lawyers union, leads a 92-strong committee of lawyers who volunteered to help him.
He repeatedly pressed witnesses over the number of Israeli tourists who came to Baqoura, how many Israeli farmers were cultivating the land, and how little control Jordanian soldiers had over them.
He also challenged Daqamsa's chances of a fair trial from a military tribunal after comments by King Hussein, supreme commander of Jordan's armed forces.

King Hussein said on March 20, one week after the shooting, that Daqamsa's action was "a mark of shame" on the army and he should have been shot dead on the spot. He travelled to Israel to pay condolences to families of the dead girls.
"Army officers are bound by their orders, so this special tribunal has lost its constitutional independence," Majalli said.
But Khasawneh rejected the defence complaint and accused Majalli of trying to turn the court into a "political pulpit".
The trial was adjourned until Wednesday.
